title: Generalization in Neural Networks Through the Lens of Magnitude Potential
claim: A standard density estimate misses sparse boundary points, while our potential-based measure captures them and mirrors a trained network's decision boundary.
layout: 4 panels in a row, left-to-right, shared red-blue colormap with colorbars
description: Four square heatmap panels in a row, labeled (a) KDE within-class, (b) MP (t = 1.0), (c) MP ratio (t = 1.0) and (d) Logit (Pre-softmax). Each panel shows the same 2-D toy dataset: a dense red cluster on the left, a dense blue cluster on the right, and a few sparse points of each class in the gap between them. The background uses a diverging red-white-blue colormap, and each panel has a colorbar on the right. In (a) the background is almost white, and the sparse boundary points are ignored. In (b), (c) and (d) the red and blue regions meet at a white boundary that bends around the sparse points. Panel (d), the neural network logit, has a boundary shape similar to (b) and (c). The eye goes first to the bending boundary in the middle panels.
caption: Comparison of KDE and MP. Each class has a cluster and a few sparse points at the boundary. (a): KDE is computed for each class, which fails to capture the sparse boundary points as it is dominated by the dense cluster. (b): MP is computed for each class, and the largest value is shown, which has a higher score at the outlier points, and shows a decision boundary similar to a neural network in (d). (c): MP ratio, which inherits this sensitivity and bends around the sparse boundary samples. (d): the pre-softmax logit of a high-accuracy model, showing similar decision boundaries.
abstract: Explaining generalization and training dynamics in neural networks remains a challenge, and various approaches have been developed to study different aspects of these phenomena. In this paper, we introduce the idea of {\em magnitude potential} -- a quantity based on the theory of metric magnitude -- that reflects how well an arbitrary point is represented by a given set. We find that this basic quantity can be applied to examine various features in neural generalization. The ratio between the magnitude potential with respect to a class and with respect to the entire data, computed at the logit layer, is informative of the representation of the point. In experiments, these ratios for individual training points are found to be correlated with the Feldman memorization scores. Magnitude potential ratios aggregated across points detect structural changes in the decision boundaries and provide a geometric indicator of grokking in modular arithmetic. Although the magnitude potential ratio and neural collapse are both closely associated with intra-class and inter-class geometric structure, the magnitude potential ratio remains informative even when neural collapse is explicitly suppressed.
